content: The initial treatment involves administering 200 mg of acyclovir orally every 4 hours while awake (5 times daily) for 10 days, or alternatively, 400 mg orally every 8 hours for 7 to 10 days. For intermittent treatment of recurrences, 200 mg is given orally every 4 hours while awake (5 times daily) for 5 days, starting at the earliest sign or symptom of recurrence. Chronic suppression for recurrent episodes can be achieved with 400 mg orally every 12 hours for up to 12 months, or alternatively, 200 mg orally 3 to 5 times daily. Intravenous (IV) administration of 10-15 mg/kg every 8 hours for 10 days, with durations of up to 14-21 days, has also been reported. In immunocompromised patients, IV dosing of 5 mg/kg every 8 hours for 7 days is recommended, with durations of up to 14 days reported. Off-label oral dosing involves 400 mg every 4 hours while awake (5 times daily) for 7 days. For acute treatment in immunocompetent patients weighing more than 40 kg, 800 mg orally every 6 hours for 5 days is recommended. In immunocompromised patients, IV dosing of 10-15 mg/kg every 8 hours for 7-10 days is used. Dose adjustments should be made based on renal clearance and the specific dosage form. Acyclovir has orphan drug designation for the treatment of herpetic keratitis. For neonates with a postmenstrual age (PMA) of ≥34 weeks, 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 21 days is recommended. For neonates with a PMA of <34 weeks, 20 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for 21 days is used. Caution is advised if renal dysfunction beyond the effects of prematurity occurs. For children aged 3 months to 12 years, 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 10 days is recommended, with durations of up to 14-21 days reported. For patients aged ≥12 years, 10-15 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 14-21 days is used. In immunocompromised patients under 12 years of age, 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 7 days is recommended. For immunocompetent patients aged ≥12 years, 800 mg orally every 4 hours while awake (5 times daily) for 7-10 days is used. For immunocompromised patients aged ≥12 years, 30 mg/kg/day IV divided every 8 hours for 7-10 days is recommended. For children aged ≥2 years and weighing <40 kg, 20 mg/kg/dose orally every 6 hours for 5 days (not exceeding 800 mg/dose) is used. For those weighing ≥40 kg, 800 mg orally every 6 hours for 5 days is recommended. Ideal body weight (IBW) should be used for dosing in obese patients. Acyclovir and amphotericin B deoxycholate both increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Concurrent use should be avoided, or alternative drugs should be considered. Similarly, acyclovir and bacitracin, cidofovir, neomycin (oral), and other nephrotoxic agents increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. These combinations should be avoided or monitored closely. Acyclovir decreases the effects of talimogene laherparepvec due to pharmacodynamic antagonism, and concurrent use should be avoided or alternative drugs considered. Acyclovir increases the levels of amoxicillin by decreasing renal clearance, and caution is advised. Co-administration with drugs like amikacin, carboplatin, cisplatin, colistin, cyclosporine, and others that increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity requires close monitoring or therapy modification. Acyclovir also increases the levels of drugs like mycophenolate and peramivir by competing for renal tubular clearance, necessitating caution and monitoring. Acyclovir interacts with various NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen) and other acidic drugs by competing for renal tubular clearance, potentially increasing their levels or effects. These interactions are generally of minor significance but should be monitored. Acyclovir also increases the levels of drugs like tenofovir and valganciclovir through similar mechanisms, requiring caution and monitoring. In summary, acyclovir has numerous drug interactions, particularly with nephrotoxic and ototoxic agents, as well as drugs that compete for renal tubular clearance. These interactions necessitate careful monitoring, dose adjustments, or the use of alternative therapies to minimize risks.
